Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without converting it into a summary judgment motion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

## ARGUMENT

### I. The District Court Properly Considered Documents Incorporated by Reference in the Complaint Without Converting the Rule 12(b)(6) Motion into One for Summary Judgment.

Review of a dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) is de novo, but the question presented here is a settled one. A court ruling on a motion to dismiss may consider materials beyond the four corners of the complaint when those materials are incorporated by reference. Doing so does not trigger Rule 12(d)'s conversion requirement.

**A. The incorporation-by-reference doctrine is well established in this Circuit.**

Rule 12(d) requires conversion only when "matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court." Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(d). This Court has long held that documents incorporated by reference in the complaint are not "outside the pleadings." A court "may . . . consider certain materials—documents attached to the complaint, documents incorporated by reference in the complaint, or matters of judicial notice—without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment." *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003). A document is incorporated by reference "if the plaintiff refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." *Id.* at 907–08; *accord Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018).

The doctrine reaches documents the complaint does not expressly quote. It extends "to situations in which the plaintiff's claim depends on the contents of a document, the defendant attaches the document to its motion to dismiss, and the parties do not dispute the authenticity of the document, even though the plaintiff does not explicitly allege the contents of that document in the complaint." *Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006); *see also Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th Cir. 2005). A court may therefore consider evidence on which the complaint "necessarily relies" when (1) the complaint refers to the document, (2) the document is central to the plaintiff's claim, and (3) no party questions its authenticity. *Marder*, 450 F.3d at 448; *Coto Settlement v. Eisenberg*, 593 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010). The doctrine also applies to material published online. *Daniels-Hall v. Nat'l Educ. Ass'n*, 629 F.3d 992, 998 (9th Cir. 2010).

Earlier decisions of this Court reached the same result. *See Branch v. Tunnell*, 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994) (documents whose contents are alleged in the complaint, and whose authenticity no party questions, may be considered on a motion to dismiss), *overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County of Santa Clara*, 307 F.3d 1119 (9th Cir. 2002).

**B. The doctrine prevents plaintiffs from evading dismissal through selective pleading.**

The doctrine protects the integrity of the pleading stage. As this Court has explained, it "prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that weaken—or doom—their claims." *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1002. A plaintiff cannot rely on a document to build a claim and then keep the document's full text out of the court's view. Consideration of the complete document does not turn the motion into a factual contest. It ensures that the court tests the claim against what the document actually says.

**C. The documents here satisfy the doctrine's requirements.**

Each document the District Court considered meets this standard. The complaint refers to each one, and Plaintiff's claims depend on their contents. [Record cites: describe each document and the complaint paragraphs that rely on it.] Plaintiff did not dispute their authenticity below. [Record cite.] Because the claims "depend[] on the contents of" these documents, *Marder*, 450 F.3d at 448, the District Court was entitled to consider them in full. Rule 12(d) did not require conversion.

**D. The District Court respected the doctrine's limits.**

Defendant does not contend that incorporation by reference permits a court to resolve factual disputes. This Court has cautioned that "it is improper to assume the truth of an incorporated document if such assumptions only serve to dispute facts stated in a well-pleaded complaint." *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1003. The District Court did not do that. It considered the documents for what they say: their terms, their text, and their context. It did not credit them to contradict Plaintiff's well-pleaded factual allegations. [Record cite.] Dismissal rested on the unambiguous content of the documents Plaintiff himself placed at issue, measured against the legal elements of his claims, and not on any disputed inference drawn in Defendant's favor.

Consideration of the incorporated documents was therefore proper under *Ritchie*, *Marder*, *Coto Settlement*, and *Khoja*. The Court should reject any argument that the District Court erred by failing to convert the motion under Rule 12(d).
